name: Elasticsearch
summary: A distributed search engine that partitions Lucene indexes into shards, coordinates scatter-gather searches, replicates shard copies with a primary-backup model, and exposes near-real-time visibility through refreshes.

features.name: Shard-partitioned Lucene index
features.description: An Elasticsearch index is divided into physical shards, each shard is a self-contained Lucene index containing a subset of documents, and shards are distributed across nodes. Lucene indexes are organized into immutable segments that are periodically merged.
benefits: Provides a unit for distributing document storage and query work across nodes
Allows each shard to use Lucene's segment-based indexing and search machinery
Makes shard placement an explicit boundary for capacity and recovery
costs: A search spanning multiple shards requires distributed coordination and result reduction
Primary shard count is fixed when an index is created
Segment merging consumes disk and other resources and can be throttled

features.name: Coordinating scatter-gather search
features.description: The node receiving a request acts as its coordinating node. For a distributed search, it resolves relevant shards, sends shard-level requests to active shard copies, and combines the returned results; the node-role documentation describes this as scatter followed by gather.
benefits: Distributes searches over the shards containing the relevant data
Presents a single client response despite multi-shard execution
Allows request coordination to be performed by any node
costs: The coordinating node must have enough resources for routing and result reduction
Network, queueing, and shard-failure behavior affect end-to-end requests
A search can return partial results when shard failures occur

features.name: Primary-replica shard replication
features.description: Each shard has a replication group with one primary shard and zero or more replica shards. The primary is the entry point for indexing, forwards accepted operations to in-sync replicas, and a replica can be promoted when the primary fails.
benefits: Provides redundant shard copies across cluster nodes
Allows an active primary or replica copy to serve reads
Defines a recovery boundary at the shard replication group
costs: Replica copies consume storage and network bandwidth
Acknowledged writes depend on the in-sync replica set and its failures
Replica promotion and recovery add coordination and operational state

features.name: Refresh-based near-real-time visibility
features.description: Elasticsearch makes indexed changes searchable through refreshes that write and open new Lucene segments without requiring a full commit. Changes are therefore not necessarily visible immediately; the documented default refresh behavior makes them visible on a near-real-time schedule for active indices.
benefits: Separates search visibility from the more expensive full commit operation
Supports frequent publication of newly indexed segments
Makes visibility timing an explicit refresh and API configuration concern
costs: A successful indexing response does not by itself mean immediate search visibility
Frequent forced refreshes can harm indexing and search behavior
Search visibility and durable commit state are distinct boundaries

features.name: Translog-backed shard recovery
features.description: Each shard copy writes index and delete operations to a transaction log after processing them in Lucene and before acknowledgement. Operations not included in the last Lucene commit can be replayed from the translog during shard recovery, subject to the configured durability and fsync boundary.
benefits: Avoids requiring a full Lucene commit for every individual operation
Provides a recovery representation for recent operations
Exposes a configurable boundary between acknowledgement, fsync, and commit
costs: Async durability can lose acknowledged operations since the last automatic commit after failure
Recovery must replay operations that are not in the last Lucene commit
Flushes and translog growth consume background resources

features.name: Shard-local query and fetch phases
features.description: Elasticsearch's search profile exposes shard-level query, collector, aggregation, and fetch phases. The query phase evaluates and collects matching documents and the fetch phase loads fields or source for selected hits; the profile is diagnostic and does not establish a fixed execution cost.
benefits: Separates matching and scoring work from retrieval of returned document data
Makes shard-local query and fetch behavior inspectable for diagnosis
Provides an evidence boundary for reasoning about distributed search execution
costs: Query, aggregation, and fetch work can vary with the request and shard contents
The coordinating node must reduce shard-level results in addition to shard-local work
Profile timings are diagnostic and should not be treated as general performance guarantees

mathematical_views.question: How does a search request become a single result from independently executed shard-level requests?
assumptions: An index is modeled as a finite set of shard partitions, each with a local search transition
The coordinating node resolves relevant shards and reduces their responses according to the request semantics
Network failures and partial results are modeled explicitly rather than assumed away

mathematical_views.question: Which shard-copy states and transitions preserve an acknowledged operation across primary and in-sync replica copies?
assumptions: A replication group consists of one primary and zero or more replica copies
The in-sync copies invariant and primary promotion are included in the state model
The view abstracts transport timing while retaining failure, demotion, and recovery transitions

mathematical_views.model: Refresh and recovery visibility state machine
mathematical_views.question: How do indexed operations move from in-memory and translog state to searchable segments and recoverable committed state?
assumptions: Search visibility is modeled separately from Lucene commit durability
Refresh, flush, translog fsync, crash, and recovery are distinct transitions
The configured translog durability mode and failure boundary are explicit parameters

mathematical_views.model: Shard-local query algebra with global reduction
mathematical_views.question: Which query, collector, aggregation, and fetch operations are evaluated locally and which results must be reduced at the coordinating node?
assumptions: Shard-local execution is represented as a partial result-producing operation
The coordinating reduction is request-specific and is not assumed to preserve every local metric directly
Profile output is treated as an execution observation, not as a performance law

benefits: Distributed storage and query capacity at shard boundaries
costs: Shard sizing, fixed primary count, and merge resource pressure

benefits: One client-facing search over distributed shard-local work
costs: Coordination resources, network dependence, and partial-result behavior

benefits: Redundant data and read-serving shard copies
costs: Replica storage, write coordination, and recovery state

benefits: Frequent search visibility without a full commit per operation
costs: Visibility delay and refresh resource trade-offs

benefits: Recoverable recent operations without committing every change to Lucene
costs: Replay work and policy-dependent failure loss windows

benefits: A separable and inspectable search execution pipeline
costs: Request- and shard-dependent execution complexity
